title: How To Encourage Your Students To Follow Rules https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2016/05/28/how-to-encourage-your-students-to-follow-rules/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin revisits the theme of explaining rules' purpose, this time grounding it in research: he cites psychologist Robert Cialdini's account, in the book Influence, of Ellen Langer's Harvard study showing that simply adding the word "because" to a request makes people more likely to comply. He applies this to classroom rules, arguing teachers should consistently frame their management plan as existing to protect students' right to learn and enjoy school, not as an act of authority. He clarifies that consistency isn't the same as strictness — it just means reliably doing what you say — and stresses that consequences should be framed as impersonal protections, never revenge or anger, reinforcing that the whole enterprise is about students, not the teacher. He previews future articles on a related strategy for prompting genuine reflection after misbehavior.
points: Citing Cialdini's Influence and Ellen Langer's Harvard study, simply adding "because" to a request measurably increases compliance.
Consistently frame classroom rules as existing to protect students' right to learn and enjoy school, not as an act of teacher authority.
Consistency is distinct from strictness — it just means reliably following through, not being harsh or authoritarian.
Enforce consequences as impersonal protections rather than revenge or anger, reinforcing that school is about the students, not the teacher.
quotes: Simply adding the word “because” makes people more likely to do what we want.
This underscores the importance of emphasizing the true purpose of your classroom management plan, which is to protect your students’ right to learn and enjoy school.
The “my way or the highway” approach misunderstands the call to be consistent with sternness, strictness, and authoritarianism.
Consistency just means that you’ll do what you say you’ll do—in this case, follow a set of guidelines that protect your students’ freedom to listen, learn, and love school.
It’s not a means of revenge or a way to express your anger. It’s simply a way to ensure a learning environment that is best for them and their education.
It further reinforces the idea that the entire enterprise, the whole point of being in school, is about them and their future.
